title: Energy Changes and Rates of Reaction
seo_title: Grade 12 Chemistry (SCH4U): Energy Changes and Rates of Reaction Worksheets (Ontario)
short_title: energy changes and rates of reaction
standard_text: Endothermic and exothermic reactions; enthalpy change; calorimetry; Hess's law and bond energies; potential-energy diagrams; collision theory, activation energy and catalysts; factors affecting rate; and rate laws. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 11 and 12: Science (2008), Chemistry, Grade 12, University Preparation (SCH4U), Strand D: Energy Changes and Rates of Reaction)
meta_desc: Free Grade 12 Chemistry (SCH4U) worksheets on energy changes and rates: enthalpy, calorimetry, Hess's law, bond energies, energy diagrams, collision theory, catalysts and rate laws. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: ΔH is negative for exothermic reactions and positive for endothermic ones.
key_sub: Rate increases with concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts.
body_html:
How to think about it

The enthalpy change ΔH is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure. In a calorimeter, q = mcΔT, and ΔH = −q ÷ n for the reaction. Hess's law: ΔH for a reaction is the same whatever the route, so you can add equations (and their ΔH). From bond energies, ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed.

Particles must collide with enough energy (the activation energy) and the right orientation. Raising the temperature, concentration or surface area increases the rate; a catalyst gives a route with a lower activation energy. A rate law has the form rate = k[A]m[B]n, with orders found by experiment.

Example

100 g of water warms by 5.0 °C in a calorimeter. Heat absorbed? (c = 4.18 J/g·°C)

q = 100 × 4.18 × 5.0

Answer: 2090 J

Example

Doubling [A] quadruples the rate. Order with respect to A?

2ⁿ = 4

Answer: second order

Common mistakes

  • Giving an exothermic ΔH a positive sign.
  • Thinking a catalyst changes ΔH: it only lowers the activation energy.
  • Reading the orders of a rate law from the balanced equation.

faq.q: Why does a higher temperature speed up a reaction?
faq.a: More particles have at least the activation energy and they collide more often.

faq.q: What does Hess's law let you do?
faq.a: Find ΔH for a reaction that is hard to measure by combining reactions with known ΔH values.

items.q: In Nathan's insulated cup, a hot lead block and cool water reach the same temperature. Which statement is true?
c: The heat lost by the metal equals the heat gained by the water.
items.e: Energy is conserved in a closed system.

items.q: Zoe mixes 100 g of water at 15 °C with 100 g of water at 69 °C in an insulated cup. What is the final temperature?
items.e: Heat lost = heat gained: (100 × 15 + 100 × 69) ÷ 200 = 42 °C.

items.q: 50.0 mL of 2.0 mol/L HCl is mixed with 50.0 mL of 2.0 mol/L NaOH. The temperature rises by 13 K. Calculate the enthalpy of neutralization (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).
items.e: q = mcΔT = 100 × 4.18 × 13 = 5520 J; n = 0.100 mol; the energy change = −q/n = −55.2 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Aiden mixes 150 g of water at 17 °C with 50 g of water at 77 °C in an insulated cup. What is the final temperature?
items.e: Heat lost = heat gained: (150 × 17 + 50 × 77) ÷ 200 = 32 °C.

items.q: In Jayden's insulated cup, a hot iron block and cool water reach the same temperature. Which statement is true?
c: The heat lost by the metal equals the heat gained by the water.
items.e: Energy is conserved in a closed system.

items.e: q = mcΔT = 100 × 4.18 × 6.4 = 2680 J; n = 0.0500 mol; the energy change = −q/n = −53.5 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Burning 0.40 g of hexane (M<sub>r</sub> 86.0) heats 150 g of water by 30.0 K. Calculate the enthalpy of combustion (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).

items.q: Burning 0.40 g of methanol (M<sub>r</sub> 32.0) heats 200 g of water by 12.0 K. Calculate the enthalpy of combustion (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).
items.e: q = mcΔT = 10000 J; n = 0.0125 mol; the energy change = −q/n = −803 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: A copper block at 80 °C is placed in water at 25 °C in a closed, insulated cup. Which final temperature is possible?
items.e: The final temperature is between the two starting temperatures.

items.q: 25.0 mL of 2.0 mol/L HCl is mixed with 25.0 mL of 2.0 mol/L NaOH. The temperature rises by 14 K. Calculate the enthalpy of neutralization (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).

items.q: 25.0 mL of 1.0 mol/L HCl is mixed with 25.0 mL of 1.0 mol/L NaOH. The temperature rises by 6.5 K. Calculate the enthalpy of neutralization (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).

items.e: Energy spreads out until temperatures are equal.

items.q: Owen drops an iron block at 90 °C into water at 18 °C. Which way does thermal energy flow?
c: from the iron to the water
both ways equally, so nothing changes
from the water to the iron
cold flows from the water into the iron
items.e: Energy flows from hot to cold.

items.q: Use these mean bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): H–H 436, N–H 391, N≡N 945. Calculate the energy change for N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub>.
items.e: the energy change = bonds broken − bonds made = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: For C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O, the energy change = −2054 kJ mol⁻¹. Mean bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): C=O 805, C–H 413, O=O 498, O–H 464. Calculate the mean bond enthalpy of the C–C bond.
items.e: the energy change = bonds broken − bonds made. Put in the known values and solve: C–C = 347.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: For N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub>, the energy change = −93 kJ mol⁻¹. Mean bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): H–H 436, N≡N 945. Calculate the mean bond enthalpy of the N–H bond.
items.e: the energy change = bonds broken − bonds made. Put in the known values and solve: N–H = 391.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Use these standard enthalpies of formation (kJ mol⁻¹): SO<sub>2</sub> −296.8, SO<sub>3</sub> −395.7. Calculate the energy change for SO<sub>2</sub> + ½O<sub>2</sub> → SO<sub>3</sub>.
items.e: the energy change = ΣΔfH(products) − ΣΔfH(reactants) = −395.7 − (−296.8) = −98.90 kJ mol⁻¹. Elements have ΔfH = 0.

items.q: Use these mean bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): Br–Br 193, H–Br 366, H–H 436. Calculate the energy change for H<sub>2</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> → 2HBr.
items.e: the energy change = bonds broken − bonds made = 629 − 732 = −103 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Use enthalpies of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹): C −393.5, H₂ −285.8, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH −1366.8. Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of ethanol (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH).
items.e: ΔfH = ΣΔcH(elements) − ΔcH(compound) = 2 × (−393.5) + 3 × (−285.8) − (−1366.8) = −277.6 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Use enthalpies of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹): C −393.5, H₂ −285.8, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> −1790.0. Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of propanone (CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>).
items.e: ΔfH = ΣΔcH(elements) − ΔcH(compound) = 3 × (−393.5) + 3 × (−285.8) − (−1790.0) = −247.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Use these mean bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 432, H–H 436. Calculate the energy change for H<sub>2</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2HCl.
items.e: the energy change = bonds broken − bonds made = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: For CH<sub>4</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O, the energy change = −818 kJ mol⁻¹. Mean bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): C=O 805, C–H 413, O–H 464. Calculate the mean bond enthalpy of the O=O bond.
items.e: the energy change = bonds broken − bonds made. Put in the known values and solve: O=O = 498.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Use these mean bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): Cl–Cl 243, C–Cl 346, C–H 413, H–Cl 432. Calculate the energy change for C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl + HCl.
items.e: the energy change = bonds broken − bonds made = 656 − 778 = −122 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Use enthalpies of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹): C −393.5, H₂ −285.8, CH<sub>4</sub> −890.30. Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of methane (CH<sub>4</sub>).
items.e: ΔfH = ΣΔcH(elements) − ΔcH(compound) = 1 × (−393.5) + 2 × (−285.8) − (−890.30) = −74.80 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Use these mean bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): Cl–Cl 243, C–Cl 346, C–H 413, H–Cl 432. Calculate the energy change for CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + HCl.
items.e: the energy change = bonds broken − bonds made = 656 − 778 = −122 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Use enthalpies of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹): C −393.5, H₂ −285.8, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> −1559.7. Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of ethane (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>).
items.e: ΔfH = ΣΔcH(elements) − ΔcH(compound) = 2 × (−393.5) + 3 × (−285.8) − (−1559.7) = −84.70 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Use these standard enthalpies of formation (kJ mol⁻¹): Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> −824.2, CO −110.5, CO<sub>2</sub> −393.5. Calculate the energy change for Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO<sub>2</sub>.
items.e: the energy change = ΣΔfH(products) − ΣΔfH(reactants) = −1180 − (−1156) = −24.80 kJ mol⁻¹. Elements have ΔfH = 0.

items.q: Use these standard enthalpies of formation (kJ mol⁻¹): C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> 52.30, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> −84.70. Calculate the energy change for C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>.
items.e: the energy change = ΣΔfH(products) − ΣΔfH(reactants) = −84.70 − (52.30) = −137.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Elements have ΔfH = 0.

items.q: Use enthalpies of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹): C −393.5, H₂ −285.8, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> −2058.0. Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of propene (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>).
items.e: ΔfH = ΣΔcH(elements) − ΔcH(compound) = 3 × (−393.5) + 3 × (−285.8) − (−2058.0) = 20.10 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Use these standard enthalpies of formation (kJ mol⁻¹): NH<sub>3</sub> −46.10, HCl −92.30, NH<sub>4</sub>Cl −314.4. Calculate the energy change for NH<sub>3</sub> + HCl → NH<sub>4</sub>Cl.
items.e: the energy change = ΣΔfH(products) − ΣΔfH(reactants) = −314.4 − (−138.4) = −176.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Elements have ΔfH = 0.

items.q: For H<sub>2</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2HCl, the energy change = −185 kJ mol⁻¹. Mean bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): Cl–Cl 243, H–H 436. Calculate the mean bond enthalpy of the H–Cl bond.
items.e: the energy change = bonds broken − bonds made. Put in the known values and solve: H–Cl = 432.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: For C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O, the energy change = −1276 kJ mol⁻¹. Mean bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): C=O 805, C–C 347, C–H 413, C–O 358, O–H 464. Calculate the mean bond enthalpy of the O=O bond.
items.e: the energy change = bonds broken − bonds made. Put in the known values and solve: O=O = 498.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Use these standard enthalpies of formation (kJ mol⁻¹): C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> 52.30, H<sub>2</sub>O −285.8, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH −277.7. Calculate the energy change for C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH.
items.e: the energy change = ΣΔfH(products) − ΣΔfH(reactants) = −277.7 − (−233.5) = −44.20 kJ mol⁻¹. Elements have ΔfH = 0.

items.q: The energy profile diagram shows a reaction. How does adding a catalyst change the diagram?
c: The products become lower in energy.
The peak is lower (smaller activation energy), but the energy change stays the same.
items.e: A catalyst gives an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.

items.q: The energy profile diagram shows a reaction. The reactants have 250 kJ/mol, the products 290 kJ/mol and the peak 410 kJ/mol. What is the energy change?
items.e: the energy change = products − reactants = 290 − 250.

items.q: The energy profile diagram shows a reaction. The reactants have 150 kJ/mol, the products 60 kJ/mol and the peak 230 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy?
items.e: Ea = peak − reactants = 230 − 150 = 80 kJ/mol.

items.q: H<sub>2</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> → 2HBr. Bond energies (kJ/mol): H–H = 436, Br–Br = 193, H–Br = 366. What is the energy change?
items.e: the energy change = broken − formed = 629 − 732 = −103 kJ.

items.q: 2NH<sub>3</sub> → N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>. Bond energies (kJ/mol): N–H = 391, N≡N = 945, H–H = 436. What is the energy change?
items.e: the energy change = broken − formed = 2346 − 2253 = +93 kJ.

items.q: A cold pack gets cold when squeezed. What is the sign of the energy change for this change?
items.e: Energy released: the energy change < 0. Energy absorbed: the energy change > 0.

items.q: Baking soda is heated to make a cake rise. Is this exothermic or endothermic?
items.e: Exothermic releases energy (surroundings warm up); endothermic absorbs energy.

items.q: The energy profile diagram shows a reaction. The reactants have 250 kJ/mol, the products 100 kJ/mol and the peak 350 kJ/mol. What is the energy change?
items.e: the energy change = products − reactants = 100 − 250.

items.q: The energy profile diagram shows a reaction. Is the reaction exothermic or endothermic?
items.e: The products are higher in energy than the reactants.

items.q: 2H<sub>2</sub>O → 2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub>. Bond energies (kJ/mol): O–H = 463, H–H = 436, O=O = 498. What is the energy change?
items.e: the energy change = broken − formed = 1852 − 1370 = +482 kJ.

items.q: Iron rusts slowly and releases a little heat. Is this exothermic or endothermic?
items.e: Exothermic releases energy (surroundings warm up); endothermic absorbs energy.

items.q: The energy profile diagram shows a reaction. What is the sign of the energy change?
items.e: Exothermic the energy change < 0; endothermic ΔH > 0.

items.q: CH<sub>4</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O. Bond energies (kJ/mol): C–H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 799, O–H = 463. Is the reaction exothermic or endothermic?
items.e: Broken 2648 kJ − formed 3450 kJ = −802 kJ.

items.q: The energy profile diagram shows a reaction. The reactants have 200 kJ/mol, the products 350 kJ/mol and the peak 450 kJ/mol. What is the energy change?
items.e: the energy change = products − reactants = 350 − 200.

items.q: Plants use light energy to make glucose in photosynthesis. What is the sign of the energy change for this change?
items.e: Energy released: the energy change < 0. Energy absorbed: the energy change > 0.

items.q: Ammonium nitrate dissolves and the water gets colder. Is this exothermic or endothermic?
items.e: Exothermic releases energy (surroundings warm up); endothermic absorbs energy.

items.q: Water is split into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity. Is this exothermic or endothermic?
items.e: Exothermic releases energy (surroundings warm up); endothermic absorbs energy.

items.q: 2HCl → H<sub>2</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub>. Bond energies (kJ/mol): H–Cl = 431, H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 242. What is the energy change?
items.e: the energy change = broken − formed = 862 − 678 = +184 kJ.

items.e: the energy change = broken − formed = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ.

items.q: Which part of the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve shows the molecules that can react?
c: the area to the right of the activation energy
the area to the left of the activation energy
the point where the curve starts
items.e: Only these molecules have enough energy.

items.q: Mei collects 250 mL of carbon dioxide in 100 s. What is the average rate of gas production?
What does 'dynamic equilibrium' mean?
c: the forward and backward rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant
there are equal amounts of reactants and products
items.e: It needs a closed system.

items.q: Ethan collects 120 mL of carbon dioxide in 80 s. What is the average rate of gas production?
One large lump of zinc is used instead of zinc granules. Which explains the change in rate?
c: Less surface area means fewer collisions.
Stirring brings fresh reactant particles together.
More surface area exposes more particles to collisions.
Slower particles collide less often and with less energy.
items.e: Collision theory.

items.q: The acid is cooled in an ice bath. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: Slower particles collide less often and with less energy.

items.q: Lucas collects 200 mL of carbon dioxide in 50 s. What is the average rate of gas production?
A reaction mixture is at equilibrium. More reactant is added. What happens?
c: the equilibrium shifts to the right
the equilibrium shifts to the left
items.e: The system uses up some of the added reactant.

items.q: Enzymes in saliva are added to starch. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: Enzymes are biological catalysts.

items.q: A catalyst is added to CO + 2H<sub>2</sub> ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>OH (making methanol) at equilibrium. What happens?
c: the equilibrium shifts to the left
the position of equilibrium does not change; equilibrium is reached faster
the equilibrium shifts to the right
items.e: A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally.

items.q: Why do most collisions not lead to a reaction?
c: the particles do not have enough energy or the right orientation
items.e: Successful collisions need E ≥ E<sub>a</sub>.

items.q: A catalyst is added to C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (hydrating ethene) at equilibrium. What happens?
c: the equilibrium shifts to the left
the position of equilibrium does not change; equilibrium is reached faster
the equilibrium shifts to the right
items.e: A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally.

A flask on a balance loses 0.5 g of gas in 25 s (Emma's experiment). What is the average rate of mass loss?
Marble chips are crushed into powder. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: More surface area exposes more particles to collisions.

items.q: The gas is squeezed into a smaller container. Which explains the change in rate?
c: Higher pressure packs gas particles closer, so they collide more often.
More particles in the same volume collide more often.
Higher oxygen concentration means more collisions.
Slower particles collide less often and with less energy.
items.e: Collision theory.

c: the equilibrium shifts to the right
the position of equilibrium does not change; equilibrium is reached faster

items.q: Mateo collects 20 mL of carbon dioxide in 10 s. What is the average rate of gas production?
Why is a high pressure expensive in industry?
c: strong equipment and lots of energy for compressors are needed
items.e: Pressures are a compromise between yield and cost.

items.q: The acid is diluted with water. Which explains the change in rate?
c: A catalyst gives a path with lower activation energy.
Less surface area means fewer collisions.

items.q: When [A] is multiplied by 3 (other concentrations fixed), the initial rate goes from 4.80 × 10<sup>−4</sup> to 4.80 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol/L s⁻¹. What is the order with respect to A?
items.e: Rate × 1 when [A] × 3: 30 = 1, so order = 0.

items.q: rate = k[A]²[B]². When [A] = 0.40 and [B] = 0.50 mol/L the rate is 0.00100 mol/L s⁻¹. Calculate k.
items.e: k = rate ÷ concentrations with their powers = 0.0250.

items.q: What are the units of k for rate = k[B]²?
items.e: Overall order 2. Units = mol/L s⁻¹ ÷ (mol/L)<sup>2</sup>.

items.q: What fraction of a first-order reactant remains after 6 half-lives?
A first-order reaction has k = 0.0230 s⁻¹. What is its half-life?
What are the units of k for rate = k[A]²[B]?
items.e: Overall order 3. Units = mol/L s⁻¹ ÷ (mol/L)<sup>3</sup>.

items.q: What are the units of k for rate = k[A][B]²?
